5-6: A part of a number known: another part of the same number.
Parts of a whole taken away, by people or on the days of a walk: what is left of it.
Fractions compared by giving them one denominator: which is bigger, or how many lie between two.
A fraction spent, then a fraction of the rest: the amount at the start.
A jug full and partly full: the weight of the jug alone.
Two parts of a whole and the difference between them: the whole.
A fraction of a fraction of a group: the part of the whole.
A strip cut into equal parts, some of them shaded: the fraction shaded, in its simplest form.
A fraction of an hour, a metre or a kilogram: the minutes, centimetres or grams it makes.
Two taps filling one tank, each alone in a known time: the part of it they fill together in an hour.
Shares of a herd of n, each over a denominator that divides n + 1 and all adding up to n parts in n + 1, as a half, a third and a ninth of 17 camels: one camel lent makes every share whole.
Cups of one size of two drinks mixed, all drunk: one person's shares of all of each drink, such as a quarter and a sixth, put the number of people strictly between those denominators, two apart.
A number taken from the numerator of a fraction and added to its denominator keeps their sum: it becomes only a fraction whose two parts add up to a divisor of that sum, as 537/463 becomes 1/9.
Things shared out equally with no piece cut into more than a few parts: each share written as a sum of fractions with 1 on top, such as 7/12 as a third and a quarter.
A trip told in parts of parts, such as asleep from halfway until half of the stretch slept is left: the part spent awake, from a drawing of the whole way.
A sum such as 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/12 + 1/20, each term 1 over two neighbours multiplied: each term is a difference of two fractions, so nearly all of them cancel.
One amount poured equally into vessels it fills to different parts, such as a half, two thirds and three quarters: the smallest whole sizes the vessels and the amount can have.
One gives another a part of a share, and the other's share grows so many times: the part of the whole each had at first.
A string of a known fractional length, such as two thirds of a metre, folded in halves and quarters: a length measured off with no ruler.
Two fractions with given denominators, such as eighths and thirteenths, unequal but as close as can be: the smallest difference is 1 over the least common multiple of the denominators.
